chapters.name: Canada's Investment Supercycle

sections.name: Making Canada the best place to invest

items.name: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction

text.topic: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
text.text: In September 2026, we announced the Productivity Mega Deduction. Building on the Productivity Super Deduction introduced last year, the Productivity Mega Deduction allows businesses to immediately write off the full cost of a broader range of capital assets, representing more than 65% of investment, on a permanent basis. This gives businesses the certainty they need to make major investment decisions, offering greater cost efficiency, competitiveness, and simplicity. Private investment in new machinery, technology, and other assets is one of the best ways to increase productivity, create jobs, and strengthen long-term growth.

text.topic: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
text.text: With the Productivity Mega Deduction, Canada's marginal effective tax rate (METR) on new business investment will fall from 13% to 6.4%—the lowest in the G7 and less than half the rate in the United States. That makes Canada more tax competitive than the U.S. across all major sectors of the economy.

text.topic: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
text.text: The Productivity Mega Deduction also gives Canada the lowest tax rate on new business investment of any major economy in the world. With an estimated fiscal cost of $36 billion over five years, beginning in 2026-27, it will help create the conditions for an extended period of higher investment: Canada's Investment Supercycle.

text.topic: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
text.text: Canada's tax advantage: lower tax rate than the U.S.

text.topic: Kickstarting Canada's Investment Supercycle with the Productivity Mega Deduction
text.text: For businesses, lower effective marginal tax rates increase the after-tax rate of return on new investment, strengthening the incentive to invest in the machinery, equipment, and technologies needed to expand production. Together with the broader package of accelerated depreciation measures introduced since Budget 2025, the Productivity Mega Deduction will support higher investment and capital accumulation across sectors, expanding the economy's productive capacity over time.

items.name: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs

text.topic: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs
text.text: Canada shares a border with one of the world's largest economic powers. To compete, we must be ambitious and ensure Canadian entrepreneurs have the opportunities, access to capital, and confidence they need to build and grow here at home.

text.topic: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs
text.text: Canadian high-growth startups drive innovation across the economy. Yet too often, their lack of access to growth capital holds them back. Talent and ideas leave Canada and take root elsewhere. To counter this, Canada must aggressively compete to attract and retain those that will create the next generation of Canadian businesses. That demands strong, pro-entrepreneurial action.

text.topic: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs
text.text: That's why Budget 2026 takes bold steps to strengthen Canada's innovation ecosystem by increasing the incentives for risk-taking, enabling successful investors and founders to reinvest in new Canadian companies while mobilising new domestic capital to support Canadian businesses. This includes:

text.topic: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs
text.text: Introducing the Canada Growth Incentive to help high-potential businesses attract investment and grow in Canada, consisting of two measures: introducing a new tax exemption for Canadian builders on up to $15 million in capital gains earned from successful investments in eligible Canadian companies and enhancing the small business rollover to allow increased deferral of taxes on capital gains when proceeds are reinvested in another Canadian small business. By allowing builders to keep more of the benefits when a business succeeds, these measures will help level the playing field with the United States, encourage more capital to flow to Canadian businesses, and enable successful entrepreneurs to reinvest their proceeds into Canada. This incentive would provide $715 million in tax relief over four years, starting in 2027-28.

text.topic: Backing Canada's next generation of entrepreneurs
text.text: Together, these measures would mean that a founder has a stronger incentive to build a valuable company in Canada, an early-stage employee sees more upside in accepting equity as part of their compensation, and an investor gets a better potential after-tax return for backing a promising Canadian company. For a founder with a $15 million capital gain, that difference is substantial: they would retain nearly 96% of the value when they exit, compared with 71% before Budget 2026.

text.topic: Helping Canadian innovators scale at home
text.text: Canada's economic security depends on innovative Canadian founders who start companies, commercialise new ideas, and scale up their businesses while remaining anchored to Canada. That is how we create good jobs at home and reap the greatest benefits from our world-class workforce and ingenuity.

text.topic: Helping Canadian innovators scale at home
text.text: Canada's Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy, first announced in Budget 2025, addresses persistent financing gaps facing Canada's most promising firms. Through up to $750 million in investments, offered on a cash basis, the Strategy will mobilise domestic private capital and help Canadian companies grow and scale right here in Canada.

items.name: Boosting innovation and commercialisation

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: Canada's research and innovation agenda is entering a pivotal phase. Major projects are moving forward at speed and scale, and significant investments are being made in research, innovation, and emerging technologies. This is a competitive advantage for Canada. We have long been a global leader in these fields, and we can fuel our long-term economic growth and competitiveness by strongly supporting science and innovation. At a time when other countries are pulling back from research, Canada is doubling down. We are putting policies in place that attract leading researchers, innovators, and entrepreneurs from around the world, giving them the opportunity to contribute here.

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: Canadian businesses need a tax system that supports businesses of all sizes, from research and development through to commercialisation. Last year, we enhanced and simplified the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program by expanding access to the enhanced credit, restoring support for capital expenditures, and increasing the annual eligible expenditure limit on which the enhanced credit can be earned to $6 million to help businesses innovate and grow. To build on this momentum:

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to further expand the SR&ED tax incentive program to include certain commercialisation expenses. Eligible expenditures would be expanded to include certain costs associated with bringing a new product or process to market, including obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications, and securing and maintaining intellectual property protection. This measure would apply to expenditures incurred in taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day. This measure is expected to provide support of $930 million over five years, with $235 million ongoing.

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: In addition, the Canada Revenue Agency will work to provide sector-specific guidance to clarify SR&ED eligibility as it pertains to commercialisation expenses.

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: The inclusion of certain commercialisation expenses under the SR&ED program will provide an additional level of support for builders and businesses performing cutting-edge research and development, translating their intellectual and technological capital into commercial-ready ventures.

items.name: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit

text.topic: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text.text: Canada hosted its first-ever Canada Investment Summit in September 2026, welcoming investors to Toronto and showcasing Canada as the destination of choice for global capital.

text.topic: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text.text: The Summit brought together investors from nearly 30 countries responsible for managing more than $100 trillion in assets, along with federal ministers, senior officials, provincial representatives, and Indigenous leaders. More than 165 investment opportunities in priority sectors—including energy and critical minerals, artificial intelligence, defence, and infrastructure—were profiled.

text.topic: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text.text: Investors immediately recognised Canada's strengths and responded to our ambitions; by the end of the Summit, nearly $500 billion in new investment commitments to Canada had been made. As a result of the government's economic plan:

text.topic: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text.text: Canada's top banks committed nearly $325 billion in new financing for Canadian businesses and infrastructure.

text.topic: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text.text: Canada's leading pension funds, insurers, and institutional investors committed nearly $100 billion in new capital to Canadian assets.

items.name: Mobilising private investment to modernise Canada's airports

text.topic: Mobilising private investment to modernise Canada's airports
text.text: Canada's airports connect Canadians and support tourism, trade, and economic growth. Airport authorities have built and maintained a safe and reliable airport system for more than three decades. In the years to come, meeting growing demand for air travel, ensuring affordability, and improving the passenger experience will require additional investment and expertise.

text.topic: Mobilising private investment to modernise Canada's airports
text.text: To prepare Canada's air transportation system for the future, we are seeking private investment through long-term operating concessions for our four largest airports. Under this model, used successfully in other countries, experienced investors, like Canada's pension funds, would operate airports for 40 to 50 years while Canada retains ownership of airport lands and assets. Operators would be subject to strong oversight to protect travellers and the interests of Canadians.

text.topic: Mobilising private investment to modernise Canada's airports
text.text: The airport fees included in the price of an airline ticket would be subject to clear rules to protect travellers from unreasonable increases. New investment and expertise will improve airport services and infrastructure—making travel more efficient and expanding travel and tourism options. Canadians will share directly in the success of concessions through equity stakes for the Canada Strong Fund and local Indigenous communities.

text.topic: Rewarding innovation by helping Canadian ideas and talent succeed
text.text: Budget 2026 will help Canadian businesses and talent succeed. Its measures will improve access to growth capital, attract world-class talent to our growing sectors, and strengthen support for research and commercialisation opportunities while protecting intellectual property. By boosting and rewarding Canadian innovation, we are helping more of our businesses start, scale, and compete worldwide.

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to further expand the SR&ED tax incentive program to include certain commercialisation expenses. Eligible expenditures would be expanded to include certain costs associated with bringing a new product or process to market, including obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications, and securing and maintaining intellectual property protection. This measure would apply to expenditures incurred in taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day. This measure is expected to provide support of $930 million over five years, with $235 million ongoing.

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: To support this, Budget 2025 announced the government's intention to undertake a performance review to strengthen Canada's intellectual property ecosystem and support the growth of intellectual-property-intensive firms. Budget 2026 announces several initial measures to deliver on that commitment, including:

text.topic: Boosting innovation and commercialisation
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $1 billion over six years, starting in 2028-29, to the Strategic Response Fund to support large-scale research and development and innovation projects that can strengthen Canada's long-term competitiveness and growth.

text.topic: Unleashing billions for Canadian businesses with the Canada Investment Summit
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $181.4 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, $50.4 million in future years, and $40.4 million ongoing to expand Invest in Canada to add specialised financial sector expertise and establish its presence in key global markets to bring in capital from major investors and multinational corporations. Invest in Canada will also deliver Canada's future Investment Summits.

text.topic: The new operating concession model for Canada's largest airports
text.text: To launch the first airport operating concession, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $37.6 million over three years, starting in 2026-27, to ensure a strong return for Canadians by completing due diligence, developing the concession framework, obtaining specialised commercial and legal advice, and completing a competitive process to select the operator by early 2029. Budget 2026 also proposes to introduce legislation necessary to implement and establish the operating concessions.

text.topic: Investing in Canada's future
text.text: Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to pursue additional measures—supported by concession proceeds—to improve the experience for travellers. These will prioritise regional connectivity, ensure air travel is affordable, and strengthen the governance and oversight of Canada's airports. Detailed measures will be developed and released over time. They will:

text.topic: Investing in Canada's future
text.text: Budget 2026 also proposes to provide $4.3 million over four years, starting in 2026-27, to Transport Canada to develop a Traveller Biometrics Strategy. The Strategy will make air travel faster and simpler, including through the potential use of digital credentials that can help travellers move through airports and other points of entry more efficiently. It will bring together airports, airlines, security screening, and border services, while protecting privacy, personal information, accessibility, cybersecurity, and individual choice. A Special Advisor on Traveller Biometrics will be appointed to lead this work and coordinate responsible and secure implementation across industry and government.

sections.name: Building a cleaner, more competitive economy

items.name: Powering Canada Strong

text.topic: Powering Canada Strong
text.text: Canada has the potential to be an energy superpower. We have abundant reserves; hydroelectric, wind, and nuclear capability; and a grid that is already among the cleanest and cheapest in the G7. Building upon this potential is how we secure our sovereignty, increase our exports, and become more self-reliant: it is, as it was for Québec when the term was first coined, an integral piece to being masters of our destiny.

text.topic: Powering Canada Strong
text.text: Electricity is key to Canada's energy security, sovereignty, and affordability; we know that the nations that master electricity will own the 21st century. Canada starts with advantages: we already have a nearly 80% clean grid and some of the lowest electricity costs among peer nations.

text.topic: Powering Canada Strong
text.text: But as our economy grows and our industries become more energy-intensive, electricity demand in Canada is expected to double by 2050. This is an enormous opportunity for Canada to build a sustainable, affordable future—but we have to start now. Increasing electrification will boost our energy sovereignty, give Canadian industries a competitive advantage, and lower energy costs for 7 in 10 Canadian families, playing a key part in the government's affordability efforts.

items.name: Growing Canada's nuclear advantage and powering our electricity future

text.topic: Growing Canada's nuclear advantage and powering our electricity future
text.text: Nuclear energy is playing a growing role around the world as countries look for reliable, low-carbon electricity to meet rising demand and strengthen their energy security. Canada has a world-class nuclear sector and is well positioned to benefit from this demand, both domestically and internationally.

text.topic: Growing Canada's nuclear advantage and powering our electricity future
text.text: Nuclear energy is essential to powering Canada's future. It provides non-emitting, dependable baseload power, backed by a strong domestic supply chain built on over 70 years of Canadian expertise, innovation, and intellectual property.

text.topic: Growing Canada's nuclear advantage and powering our electricity future
text.text: Today, the nuclear sector is responsible for 90,000 direct and indirect jobs, and in the nuclear industry itself, 90% of jobs are in high-skilled roles. Nuclear energy contributes 13% of our national electricity supply, and it adds $22 billion to Canada's economy every year through the operation of 17 Canada Deuterium Uranium (CANDU) reactors at home and the servicing of nine reactors abroad in countries like Romania, India, and South Korea. We are committed to keeping this Canadian technology market-ready for use at home and in international markets.

items.name: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure

text.topic: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure
text.text: As more Canadians choose zero-emission vehicles, demand for electric vehicle chargers will continue to grow. Within five years, EV sales are projected to reach nearly 40% of global car sales. We have invested steadily to expand the charging network by supporting more than 50,000 chargers to date. A larger network makes it easier and more convenient for Canadians to drive electric vehicles, particularly in rural communities, helping Canada become a global leader in vehicle electrification.

text.topic: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure
text.text: Budget 2026 builds on this progress achieved, with the ambition to roughly double the number of federally supported chargers, making it easier for Canadian drivers to save money, plan their routes, and travel in confidence:

text.topic: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure
text.text: To support the installation of over 55,000 additional EV chargers in areas where the infrastructure is needed most, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $587 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to Environment and Climate Change Canada to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program.

text.topic: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure
text.text: To fund research and development for charging infrastructure, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $45 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to Natural Resources Canada. This funding would help bring innovative Canadian EV charging solutions to market, delivering more affordable, reliable, and accessible EV charging solutions that work for Canadians, businesses, and the electricity grid.

text.topic: Expanding Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure
text.text: To support the transition of the federal fleet to zero-emission vehicles, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $2.2 million over five years, starting in 2027-28, to renew the Greening Government Operations Fleet Program, which conducts readiness assessments to support the transition of the federal vehicle fleet to zero-emission vehicles.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: To provide the certainty needed for longer-term projects, Budget 2026 proposes to extend the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits to the end of 2040. For the Clean Technology investment tax credit, the phase-out to 15% would occur in 2040 rather than 2034.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: To encourage more investment in electricity transmission, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligibility for the Clean Electricity investment tax credit to the highest-voltage intra-provincial electricity transmission lines in each province, for property acquired and available for use on or after Budget Day.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: In addition, Budget 2026 proposes further investments to expand, strengthen, and better connect Canada's electricity systems.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: To deliver more reliable power as electricity demand grows, Budget 2026 proposes to provide nearly $4 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28. This funding will support electricity infrastructure expansion, renewable energy, and priority electricity sector projects across Canada, including new funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: Our electricity grids in Canada are currently far too fragmented. Stronger interties can better connect electricity systems across Canada, allowing electricity to move more easily across provincial and territorial borders. Budget 2026 proposes to provide $37 million in 2027-28 to support robust cost-benefit analysis of proposed interties and inform cross-border cost-allocation discussions.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: To support the allocation of investment for Canada's electricity system buildout, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $26.4 million over 10 years (on a cash basis) to Natural Resources Canada for data and modelling capacity to improve system planning and help guide investments where they will be most beneficial. Budget 2026 also proposes to provide $22.9 million over five years to Environment and Climate Change Canada to update the Clean Electricity Regulations and to develop equivalency agreements with provinces and territories where appropriate.

text.topic: EV chargers to be installed by 2028-29
text.text: To improve energy reliability in the North, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $1.6 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28. This includes $713.8 million for renewable energy and capacity-building projects that help Indigenous, rural, and remote communities transition from diesel and fossil fuels to renewable energy sources, and $929.1 million to replace and upgrade aging electricity infrastructure in northern communities. This funding will support the Mayo Hydro Facility and Atlin Hydro Expansion projects.

text.text: To realise this opportunity, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $6 billion over six years, starting in 2028-29, earmarked to support the deployment of emerging electricity generation technologies.

text.topic: Bringing critical minerals from mine to market
text.text: Canada stands as a global leader in mining and critical minerals, such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and rare earth elements that are used in batteries, electric vehicles, and other clean technologies. We are known around the world for our mining schools, for our expertise and technology, and for the reliability we offer as a mining nation. But for too long, Canada has fallen behind in bringing those minerals from mine to market. That is why we are focused on increasing Canadian production and processing of our minerals.

items.name: Strengthening Canada's forest sector

text.topic: Strengthening Canada's forest sector
text.text: Canada has a world-renowned forest sector. It is the bedrock of hundreds of rural, remote, and Indigenous communities, employs nearly 200,000 workers, and is a staple of Canadian resource exports. In 2025, the sector contributed $29.7 billion to Canada's GDP.

text.topic: Strengthening Canada's forest sector
text.text: Due to unjustified U.S. tariffs, changing global markets, and shifting wood product needs, our forest sector is facing significant pressures. The sector must improve its productivity and competitiveness to keep pace. That is why we are supporting and strengthening Canada's forest industry for the challenges of today and the demands of the future in Budget 2026. It proposes:

text.topic: Strengthening Canada's forest sector
text.text: $500 million over six years, starting in 2027-28, to Natural Resources Canada, to strengthen fibre supply chains and support provinces, territories, Indigenous partners, and industry in advancing forest management and stewardship, and deploying new technologies and practices.

text.topic: Strengthening Canada's forest sector
text.text: $2 billion over six years, starting in 2027-28, to Natural Resources Canada to help businesses in the forest sector modernise facilities and equipment, improve productivity, and expand production of higher-value products, as well as to support research, development, and demonstration projects.

text.topic: Strengthening Canada's forest sector
text.text: $4 billion over six years, starting in 2027-28, on a cash basis, to Export Development Canada through the Canada Account to support a new Forestry Sector Accelerator to make investments in new large-scale facilities and in major transformations of existing facilities, including biorefineries, biofuel facilities, and other facilities producing higher-value and innovative forest products.

text.topic: Canada–Ukraine Cooperation Agreement in Geoscience
text.text: To build on this progress and unlock more of Canada's critical minerals potential, Budget 2026 proposes to:

text.topic: Canada–Ukraine Cooperation Agreement in Geoscience
text.text: Renew the Canadian Critical Minerals Strategy, which supports strategic investments in the technology needed to mine and process our critical minerals, expands our geoscience and research capacity, provides targeted funding for priority critical minerals projects, and keeps government priorities aligned with market needs. Budget 2026 proposes to provide Natural Resources Canada with $424.4 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, to support this renewal.

text.topic: Canada–Ukraine Cooperation Agreement in Geoscience

text.topic: Moving major projects forward faster
text.text: For too long, nation-building infrastructure in Canada was bogged down in red tape, leaving enormous investments on the table. The path to approval was confusing and overlapping, and the onus was on the proponent to navigate the system.

text.topic: Moving major projects forward faster
text.text: In August 2025, Canada's new government changed that by establishing the Major Projects Office to streamline and accelerate regulatory approval processes and help structure and coordinate project financing.

text.topic: Moving major projects forward faster
text.text: The Major Projects Office is working. Canada is working. Since September 2025, 28 nation-building initiatives have been referred to the Major Projects Office that position Canada for growth in broad sectors like electricity, nuclear energy, liquefied natural gas, critical minerals, and transportation infrastructure. The Office is doing this in full partnership with Indigenous Peoples, and while protecting the environment.

text.topic: Moving major projects forward faster
text.text: The 18 projects referred to the Major Projects Office have clear proponents and require federal coordination and support to succeed; collectively, these represent more than $194 billion in new investments, estimated to support 200,000 jobs per year during the construction phase. The 10 transformative strategies are early-stage initiatives that would strengthen Canada's economy.

text.topic: Moving major projects forward faster
text.text: To advance these efforts, we introduced Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, in September 2026. It establishes a "one project, one decision, one year" approach to federal approvals. Consultations will be coordinated through a single federal process, reducing duplication and consultation fatigue while supporting more meaningful, rights-based dialogue. That is how we get projects built faster and strengthen Canada's trade corridors and ports, supporting our workers in Canada's federally regulated sectors.

text.topic: Supporting major projects across the country
text.text: As we continue to move major projects forward faster, we are supporting projects at different stages of development. text.topic: Supporting major projects across the country

text.topic: Providing more help with groceries and everyday essentials
text.text: Building a stronger economy will deliver lasting benefits for Canadians, but those gains will take time. Right now, many families are still feeling the pressure of high grocery bills and other everyday costs.

text.topic: Providing more help with groceries and everyday essentials
text.text: To provide more support now, we introduced the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit. This benefit provides quarterly support to more than 12 million individuals and families with low or modest incomes, and is indexed annually to keep pace with the cost of living. Introduced in January 2026 to help offset higher food costs, this benefit has continued to provide additional relief, with a one-time 50% top-up in June 2026 and a 25% increase in the benefit for five years beginning in July 2026. To provide more help with the cost of groceries and other essentials:

text.topic: Providing more help with groceries and everyday essentials
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to enhance this benefit again through the 2027 Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit Supplement, which would provide a one-time 50% increase for the 2026-27 benefit year, delivered in early 2027. The Supplement would provide up to $339 for a single person without children and up to $679 for a couple with two children. Combined with the June 2026 top-up and the 25% increase in the benefit as of July 2026, this supplement would bring total support in 2026-27 to up to about $1,290 for a single person without children and $2,570 for a couple with two children. It would provide $4.1 billion in additional support to Canadians and is expected to lift an additional 120,000 people out of poverty in 2027.

text.topic: Providing more help with groceries and everyday essentials
text.text: Budget 2026 also expands and stabilises funding for Nutrition North Canada and associated initiatives, which help lower the cost of imported foods and support local food harvesting and distribution initiatives in remote northern communities.

text.topic: Strengthening support for workers earning low wages
text.text: Working should give people a real chance to build a good life and get ahead, but for many Canadians earning lower wages, everyday costs can still put that goal out of reach. The Canada Workers Benefit provides a refundable tax credit to supplement the earnings of about 3 million low- and modest-income workers each year. This helps them work and contribute to Canada's economy while giving them the boost they need to keep enough money in their pockets.

text.topic: Strengthening support for workers earning low wages
text.text: However, the existing minimum earnings threshold of $3,000 per year means some people with very low earnings do not qualify, despite being workers. Recipients also automatically receive part of the following year's benefit in advance, based on their entitlement from the previous year. This means when their circumstances change, some may receive advance payments that exceed the support they ultimately qualify for.

text.text: As Canadians, we take care of each other when help is needed. Caregivers, both paid and unpaid, provide essential support to Canadians with health conditions. More than half of Canadian women are caregivers, with about one quarter of women providing unpaid care to adults with long-term medical conditions or disabilities. These caregivers help family, friends, and people in need remain in their homes and communities.

text.topic: Making the Canada Caregiver Credit refundable
text.text: However, many caregivers have incomes too low to pay tax and therefore do not fully benefit from the existing Canada Caregiver Credit. text.topic: Lowering costs for Canadians at the pump
text.text: Global conflict and ongoing supply disruptions in the Middle East are driving up fuel prices around the world. To help Canadians and businesses manage the rising costs of fuel, we temporarily suspended the federal fuel excise tax on gasoline, diesel fuel, and aviation fuels, effective April 20, 2026.

text.topic: Lowering costs for Canadians at the pump
text.text: This suspension reduced Canadians' bills at the pump by up to 10 cents per litre on regular gasoline and up to 4 cents on diesel.

text.topic: Lowering costs for Canadians at the pump
text.text: In September 2026, we announced that this temporary tax relief would be extended until the end of January 2027. Fuel excise tax rates will then be restored to 50% of their pre-suspension levels until the end of March 2027, before returning to their standard rates on April 1, 2027. This is a responsible measure that addresses a root cause of affordability challenges for Canadians now—the cost of transportation—while balancing fiscal prudence.

text.topic: Lowering costs for Canadians at the pump
text.text: Extending the tax relief into early 2027 lowers costs at the pump and across supply chains. It provides important relief to truckers and businesses in the food, agriculture, housing, construction, and delivery sectors. For Canadians, it means continuing to save more than $5 every time they fill a typical 50-litre tank of gasoline while the full relief remains in place. The extension is expected to provide an additional $2.9 billion in fuel tax relief, bringing total estimated tax relief for Canadians to $5.3 billion in 2026-27.

text.topic: Lowering costs for Canadians at the pump
text.text: Heating is one of the biggest expenses for Canadians during the winter months, and too often, that money goes to the most expensive and least efficient ways to heat a home. Over seven million households in Canada still heat their homes with oil, propane, diesel, electric baseboards, or outdated furnaces, leaving many families with excessively high energy bills. We are working to give Canadians more choice over how they heat and cool their homes and more control over what they pay for energy.

text.topic: Pillar 1: Putting Canada on a path to end homelessness in 10 years
text.text: Canada has the resources, the people, and the will to end homelessness—but every level of government and each sector has a role to play. It requires forward-thinking action: stable housing and a comprehensive set of services—including health care, mental health and addictions treatment, crisis services, and other community supports. We are committed to changing how Canada addresses homelessness and supports those who are unhoused, because every Canadian should have the security of a warm home. That is why Budget 2026 is putting significant federal resources toward helping create the conditions to end homelessness within 10 years. This is a call to action for every level of government, Indigenous partners, the private sector, and the not-for-profit sector to come together to reach this goal.

text.topic: Pillar 1: Putting Canada on a path to end homelessness in 10 years
text.text: Homelessness remains one of Canada's most urgent social challenges. But homelessness is not inevitable. It is the result of gaps across housing, health, mental health, addictions, and social support systems. Addressing it requires coordinated action from all levels of government, Indigenous partners, service providers, communities, and the private and public sectors. Budget 2026 proposes a renewed partnership: one in which the federal government invests capital in housing and infrastructure, while provinces and territories will take the lead in ongoing operations and wraparound services, like health care and mental health and substance abuse supports.

text.topic: Pillar 1: Putting Canada on a path to end homelessness in 10 years
text.text: Budget 2026 sets Canada on a path to end homelessness over the next decade through strong measures to provide help, housing, and health to Canadians experiencing homelessness.

text.topic: Pillar 1: Putting Canada on a path to end homelessness in 10 years
text.text: Help: We will work closely with provinces, municipalities, and philanthropy to provide the help people need as they transition from experiencing homelessness and find a permanent home. This includes jobs, training, and income supports.

text.topic: Pillar 1: Putting Canada on a path to end homelessness in 10 years
text.text: Housing: As part of this plan, the Government of Canada is making a historic, multi-billion-dollar investment to build the transitional and permanent housing necessary to pragmatically ending the homelessness crisis.

text.topic: Pillar 2: Expand non-market housing
text.text: Over the past several decades, the growth of Canada's non-market housing supply has simply not kept pace with Canadians' housing needs. As a result, non-market housing today represents only a small share of Canada's housing stock, at about 4%. Budget 2026 charts a new course to triple the pace of non-market housing starts in Canada to 24,000 non-market housing starts each year over the next decade.

text.topic: Pillar 2: Expand non-market housing
text.text: By boosting the capital of Build Canada Homes, unlocking federal lands, leveraging private and philanthropic investment, and working in partnership with provinces and territories, we will work to significantly increase annual non-market housing construction. The goal is not simply to fund more projects, but to build a permanent housing delivery system capable of producing affordable homes at scale. To that end:

text.topic: Pillar 2: Expand non-market housing
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide an additional $13 billion over ten years, on a cash basis, starting in 2028-29, to boost the capital of Build Canada Homes and supercharge non-market housing across this country. All told, the investments in this Budget will set Build Canada Homes on a path to deliver 200,000 new homes across the country in the next decade, making its total capitalisation $45 billion. At least 10% of Build Canada Homes' expanded envelope will be dedicated to Indigenous housing projects using a distinctions-based formula.

items.name: Turning federal lands and buildings into homes

text.topic: Turning federal lands and buildings into homes
text.text: Federal land is significantly underused as the basis for new homebuilding in Canada. Putting underused federal land to work for housing can lower development costs and make it easier to build homes at more affordable prices, while ensuring valuable public assets deliver greater benefit for Canadians. Budget 2026 strengthens Build Canada Homes' ability to unlock federal land with the recent decision to incorporate elements of the Canada Lands Company Limited. This will bring land, development expertise, and housing investment under one roof, allowing federal properties to move more quickly from identification to construction. In addition to this expanded mandate:

text.topic: Turning federal lands and buildings into homes
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $1.5 billion over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $387.4 million in future years to prepare federal lands for housing by funding water, wastewater, roads, and other enabling infrastructure. This investment will help turn underused federal properties into complete communities and lower the cost of delivering affordable homes.

items.name: Pillar 3: Building a housing market that works for all

text.topic: Pillar 3: Building a housing market that works for all
text.text: Central to the government's affordability mission is a simple premise: building more homes, at a generational scale and speed, to bring costs down for Canadians. But building homes faster cannot happen by relying on old methods. It requires innovative new approaches to how housing is planned and constructed so that the workers, time, equipment, and materials currently available work efficiently and produce more homes. This is why we are focused on increasing housing construction productivity: better coordination, greater use of modern tools and building methods, and fewer costs and obstacles that slow down construction, including unnecessary fees, levies, taxes, and development charges.

text.topic: Pillar 3: Building a housing market that works for all
text.text: Today, the homebuilding sector produces fewer homes for each worker than it did two decades ago. Canadians expect better, and the opportunity to reverse that trend is substantial. If Canada's residential construction sector could build as efficiently as it did two decades ago, the gains would be equivalent to adding up to 150,000 additional housing starts per year.

text.topic: Pillar 3: Building a housing market that works for all
text.text: We have already taken action to help unlock more housing supply. Through the Improving Housing Supply Act (Bill C-26), the government provided provinces and territories with a $1.7 billion one-time payment, while a new partnership with Ontario is helping cut taxes on housing to boost supply, reducing the cost of a home by up to $200,000. We are also working with communities to lower development charges, which will, in turn, decrease the cost of homebuilding through the Build Communities Strong Fund.

text.topic: Pillar 3: Building a housing market that works for all
text.text: There are encouraging signs of progress. In Ontario, new data tracked by the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD) shows that more than 8,400 new homes were sold between April and June, compared with about 3,600 over the same period in 2025, an increase of more than 130%.

text.topic: Pillar 3: Building a housing market that works for all
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes $100 million over three years, starting in 2027-28, toward a partnership with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to support municipal e-permitting and the adoption of artificial intelligence, enabling more efficient and effective review and approval processes, to get homes built faster. Already, municipalities are demonstrating the efficiencies gained from digital and AI-enabled permitting: in Edmonton, Alberta, automated reviews have reduced approval times from two weeks to just one day.

items.name: Helping Canadians get an affordable mortgage

text.topic: Helping Canadians get an affordable mortgage
text.text: For many Canadians, buying a home is one of life's biggest milestones, and the largest financial commitment they will ever make. Yet the mortgage process is often unclear, leaving too many prospective buyers facing challenges understanding how much they can afford, navigating the mortgage application process, comparing mortgage rates and terms, and finding the mortgage that best meets their needs. Buying a home must be made less difficult for Canadians. A simpler, more transparent mortgage process will help Canadians make informed decisions and find more affordable options.

text.topic: Helping Canadians get an affordable mortgage
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes several measures to make this process easier and more transparent, while giving Canadians greater choice and flexibility when shopping for a mortgage:

text.topic: Helping Canadians get an affordable mortgage
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to establish new regulations to enhance publicly available information on insured mortgage rates, to be published by the Bank of Canada. Better and more timely information will help borrowers compare and shop for the best available rates.

text.topic: Helping Canadians get an affordable mortgage
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to amend the Canada Revenue Agency Act to provide the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) with the authority to enter into agreements with mortgage lenders and mortgage insurers to provide an income verification service. This service would make the mortgage application process more reliable and efficient while helping to deter mortgage fraud. Budget 2026 proposes to provide $13 million to the CRA over three years, starting in 2027-28, to develop and pilot the service. Following this initial phase, we intend for the service to be supported through funding arrangements with industry.

text.topic: Helping Canadians get an affordable mortgage
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to amend mortgage insurance rules to raise the home price limit for optional mortgage insurance from $1 million to $1.5 million and permit 30-year amortisations for these insured mortgages, provided that at least one borrower is a first-time home buyer or the home is newly built. These changes would encourage greater competition between lenders and give home buyers more flexibility.

text.topic: Securing a resilient food supply chain
text.text: Canada is one of the largest exporters of agri-food products in the world. Yet Canadians, like people in many other G7 countries, continue to face high levels of food price inflation. Currently, there is not enough competition in the grocery sector; we are not harnessing enough technology in our agri-food sectors; and our food chains rely too heavily on foreign suppliers.

text.topic: Securing a resilient food supply chain
text.text: To change this, in June 2026 we launched Canada's first-ever National Food Security Strategy. The Strategy puts Canadians back in control of what we grow, what we buy, and what we put on our tables, effectively addressing one of the biggest drivers of affordability concerns for Canadians.

text.topic: Pillar 1: Putting Canada on a path to end homelessness in 10 years
text.text: Homelessness remains one of Canada's most urgent social challenges. But homelessness is not inevitable. It is the result of gaps across housing, health, mental health, addictions, and social support systems. Addressing it requires coordinated action from all levels of government, Indigenous partners, service providers, communities, and the private and public sectors. Budget 2026 proposes a renewed partnership: one in which the federal government invests capital in housing and infrastructure, while provinces and territories will take the lead in ongoing operations and wraparound services, like health care and mental health and substance abuse supports.

The Fund would also help develop new transitional and supportive housing, adapt existing buildings, and mobilise public, private, and philanthropic capital behind an integrated housing and care model.

text.topic: Help people move from homelessness into stable housing:
text.text: Budget 2026 also proposes to provide an additional $3.6 billion over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $6.4 billion in future years, through Build Canada Homes to build new supportive and transitional housing across Canada. More details on the enhanced initiative will be released early in the new year.

text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to extend the ban on foreign purchases of existing residential properties for two years, to January 1, 2029, while exempting new residential properties. text.text: Budget 2026 announces that the government is delivering on the commitment in the Spring Economic Update 2026 to change mortgage insurance rules to help unlock financing for "missing middle" homes. text.text: A homebuilder plans to construct a $3 million fourplex in their community, adding four new homes to the local housing supply. text.text: In addition to implementing the National Food Security Strategy, making the National School Food Program permanent, and providing $20 million to the Local Food Infrastructure Fund for food banks, Budget 2026 proposes targeted support to help keep food costs down. items.name: Improving access to mental health and home and community care

text.topic: Improving access to mental health and home and community care
text.text: Canada's universal health care system is a source of national pride and a cornerstone of Canadian identity. When Canadians can get the care they need, when and where they need it, everyone benefits.

text.topic: Improving access to mental health and home and community care
text.text: Since 2018-19, the federal government has provided $11 billion to improve access to quality mental health and addictions services, as well as home care and community care, through bilateral agreements with provinces and territories. These supports have been crucial to helping Canadians access the care they need, regardless of their ability to pay.

text.topic: Improving access to mental health and home and community care
text.text: To address immediate needs in mental health and home and community care delivery, Budget 2026 proposes to:

text.topic: Improving access to mental health and home and community care
text.text: Provide $1.2 billion in 2027-28 to extend federal funding agreements with the provinces and territories for mental health and addictions services, as well as home and community care, until March 31, 2028.

text.topic: Improving access to mental health and home and community care
text.text: Extending this funding will help relieve immediate pressures on provincial and territorial health care systems while creating the conditions for a structured dialogue on the long-term productivity and sustainability of health care systems across Canada. Through a spirit of cooperative federalism, this collaboration can help support a more sustainable, efficient, and responsive health care system for Canadians.

items.name: Renewing the Emergency Treatment Fund

text.topic: Renewing the Emergency Treatment Fund
text.text: The illegal drug crisis takes the lives of an average of 15 Canadians per day, straining Canada's communities, health care systems, and social services. The government is working with communities across the country to respond to this crisis and connect people with the life-saving services and supports they need.

text.topic: Renewing the Emergency Treatment Fund
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $100 million over two years, starting in 2027-28, to renew Health Canada's Emergency Treatment Fund. The Fund supports locally driven responses to urgent substance use and overdose needs, including mobile outreach, naloxone distribution, and land-based healing programs in municipalities and Indigenous communities across Canada.

items.name: Improving access to medications

text.topic: Improving access to medications
text.text: Canadians depend on timely access to critical vaccines and life-saving medicines that keep us safe and healthy and allow us to be active members of our communities. Canadians need to know that treatment will be available when it matters most, whether the medicine is made here in Canada or abroad.

text.topic: Improving access to medications
text.text: In June 2026, the Pharmaceutical and Life Sciences Sector Task Force launched by the ministers of Health and Industry published a final report with 39 recommendations to improve access to medicines and support a strong and competitive pharmaceutical and life sciences industry. The government is currently assessing the Task Force's recommendations; further details will be announced in the coming months.

text.topic: Improving access to medications
text.text: In the meantime, Budget 2026 is taking steps to support health research into new medical treatments, by proposing to provide $10 million over two years, starting in 2027-28, to the Praxis Spinal Cord Institute, to help it develop new treatments for life-altering medical conditions.

text.topic: Supporting a healthy and secure future
text.text: Budget 2026 will help Canadians make informed financial decisions, reduce unnecessary costs, and improve access to essential care and medications. Government action will ensure that people have the information, protection, and services they need to navigate their finances with better certainty, helping them respond to unexpected challenges.

text.text: Budget 2026 proposes additional practical protections to make prices and financial products easier to understand, cut unnecessary borrowing costs, and help Canadians as they manage their budgets.

text.topic: Supporting Canadians as they manage their budgets
text.text: Canadians should not have to search through complex documents just to understand the costs of their everyday banking. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to develop regulations requiring banks to provide consumers with a single clear annual statement of the fees paid on their chequing and savings accounts, as is currently the case in the European Union and the United Kingdom. By consolidating and calculating the true costs of an account, banking costs will become easier to understand, helping Canadians choose the accounts that best fit their needs.

text.text: When a credit card balance carries more than one interest rate, every dollar paid should contribute to paying down the most expensive debt first. Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to consult on legislative amendments that would require credit card payments above the minimum amount to be applied first to balances carrying the highest interest rate, as is currently practised in Québec. This would help Canadians pay down credit card debt faster and save on interest.

sections.name: Growing our skilled workforce to build Canada Strong

items.name: Launching Team Canada Strong

text.topic: Launching Team Canada Strong
text.text: Canada's nation-building agenda depends on the men and women who build the homes, transportation networks, energy systems, defence infrastructure, and industrial projects that will drive growth for decades to come. To replace retiring workers and meet growing demand, more than 1.4 million people will be needed in Canada's skilled trades by 2033.

text.topic: Launching Team Canada Strong
text.text: That is why we announced Team Canada Strong in the Spring Economic Update 2026. Our plan is to recruit, train, and hire this next generation of skilled men and women, with the goal of adding up to 100,000 new Red Seal skilled trades workers by 2031. It's a win-win-win proposition: more Canadians, including young Canadians just starting out, will find it possible to pursue rewarding careers.

text.topic: Launching Team Canada Strong
text.text: Employers will have access to talented, well-trained workers. And the major projects that benefit Canada will get built. This ambitious goal will be met by creating clearer pathways into skilled trades through paid work placements, offering better income support during training, and providing incentives to complete apprenticeships and earn Red Seal certification. It will also reduce barriers to labour mobility so that workers can pursue opportunities wherever their skills are needed.

text.topic: Launching Team Canada Strong
text.text: Achieving Team Canada Strong's ambition of adding up to 100,000 new Red Seal skilled trades workers by 2031 will require breaking down barriers that prevent women from entering and advancing in the trades. Across Canada, unions and community organisations are already leading by example.

text.topic: Launching Team Canada Strong
text.text: The Labourers' International Union of North America (LiUNA) is combining hands-on training with advocacy for properly fitting safety equipment, clean and private washrooms, and better child care supports, while its women-led POWER initiative promotes safer, more inclusive workplaces.

text.topic: Helping workers build skills for the jobs of tomorrow
text.text: Canada's labour market is evolving rapidly. New technologies and shifts in the global economy are changing the skill sets employers need while also creating new opportunities for workers throughout their careers.

text.topic: Helping workers build skills for the jobs of tomorrow
text.text: To meet these changing conditions, Canadian workers and employers must adapt. Workers need access to training and employment supports to develop new skills, transition between jobs, and pursue rewarding opportunities in growing sectors. Businesses need access to talented, skilled men and women to innovate, invest, and expand their operations.

text.topic: Helping workers build skills for the jobs of tomorrow
text.text: We have already acted through Workforce Alliances, supports for workers affected by trade disruptions, and measures to improve and streamline the recognition of foreign credentials. Budget 2026 builds on these efforts by strengthening workforce development for Indigenous workers. This includes:

text.topic: Helping workers build skills for the jobs of tomorrow
text.text: Launching a new Partnerships for Indigenous Workforce Readiness Fund. Alongside the existing Indigenous Skills and Employment Training Program, the Fund would continue to support foundational skills and employment training through Indigenous service delivery organisations and provide a streamlined and flexible mechanism to align Indigenous workforce investments with national economic priorities. Budget 2026 proposes to provide $451.8 million over four years beginning in 2027-28, and $48 million ongoing (including new and existing funding) to launch the Fund.

text.topic: Helping workers build skills for the jobs of tomorrow
text.text: We are also working on an Indigenous-focused stream of the Team Canada Strong initiative to connect Indigenous workers with paid, entry-level trades jobs and get them onto job sites faster. Together, these measures help more Canadians succeed in the labour market and ensure Canadian businesses and major projects have access to the skilled workforce needed to advance Canada's economic priorities.

text.topic: Helping workers affected by tariffs gain new skills
text.text: As trade disruptions continue to adversely impact many Canadians' livelihoods, it is imperative that they be supported in the short term while they acquire the skills needed for tomorrow. Through targeted response measures, we can make the pathways for adapting, retraining, and moving into new positions significantly more accessible for our workers. That provides the immediate certainty, at home and at work, that Canadian workers need as they adapt to changing circumstances beyond our borders.

text.topic: Helping workers affected by tariffs gain new skills
text.text: To support Canadian workers affected by tariffs and other disruptions in trade, we introduced $3.5 billion in Rapid Response Supports for Workers and Employers in August 2026. This includes the new Worker Retention and Retraining Program to help employers keep and retrain their workforce through a difficult period.

text.text: In response to the uncertainty brought on by ongoing trade disruptions, some affected workers may decide to upgrade their skills. Budget 2026 proposes to help make this a more accessible and affordable option for Canadians who wish to do so:

text.text: Immigration has been fundamental to who we are as a country and will be important to how we build for our future. Immigrants have built and shaped our past, from helping to settle communities to building leading businesses and advancing scientific discovery. They continue to strengthen our communities, economy, and culture. In exchange for benefiting from the talent, ideas, and entrepreneurship that newcomers bring to our country, Canada has a responsibility to ensure that the people we welcome as our workers and neighbours can build successful, productive lives here. A well-managed immigration system does both.

text.topic: Celebrating Canada's 160th anniversary
text.text: Building on the legacy of Canada 150, Canada 160 celebrations will bring together the stories, spaces, and experiences that strengthen national pride and belonging, and leave a lasting legacy in communities across the country. Canada 160 is an invitation to every Canadian to read and tell our stories, gather in the places that bring us together, and celebrate what it means to be Canadian.

text.topic: Celebrating Canada's 160th anniversary
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $300 million in 2027-28 for a suite of programs that will support the stories, spaces, and experiences that bring Canadians together. The Canada 160 Fund will be a flagship initiative to mark Canada's 160th anniversary. The Fund will support signature experiences to celebrate this anniversary, support the iconic Heritage Minutes, the Trans Canada Trail—the world's longest hiking network spanning over 30,000 kilometres—and fund community spaces through an existing $100 million sourced through the Build Communities Strong Fund.

text.topic: Celebrating Canada's 160th anniversary
text.text: Festivals, hometown games, concerts, and community celebrations turn local connections into lasting memories. They bring together people who might otherwise never meet, across regions, generations, languages, and backgrounds, and remind us of all that we share in common as Canadians.

text.topic: Celebrating Canada's 160th anniversary
text.text: As we mark Canada's 160th anniversary, we want to celebrate the communities that have shaped our country and continue to define who we are today. From the Moosehide Gathering in Yukon, to the Festival Western de St-Tite in Québec, to the Deer Lake Strawberry Festival in Newfoundland and Labrador, these festivals give life to communities, and offer Canadians an opportunity to come together and celebrate the history, traditions, and people that make their communities unique.

text.topic: Celebrating Canada's 160th anniversary
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $10 million in 2027-28 for the Building Communities through Arts and Heritage program and $15 million for the Canada Arts Presentation Fund, to support local festivals and performing arts events across Canada in honour of Canada's 160th anniversary.

items.name: Revitalising recreational facilities and ice rinks

text.topic: Revitalising recreational facilities and ice rinks
text.text: Arenas, ice rinks, and recreational facilities are at the heart of many communities across Canada. They are where so many Canadians first learn to skate, where young Canadians gather after school and adults lace up after work, and where families and friends huddle in the stands for the sports they love. But many of these facilities are aging and need significant investment to remain safe, accessible, and ready to serve their communities for years to come. To renew these important community spaces:

text.topic: Revitalising recreational facilities and ice rinks
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $1.5 billion over nine years through the Build Communities Strong Fund to support the construction, expansion, retrofit, and rehabilitation of community recreational facilities and ice rinks across Canada. This includes $750 million for the ice rinks and $750 million in additional funding for other community recreational facilities. These investments will help extend the life of aging facilities and ensure communities have modern, welcoming places to come together, compete, and play.

items.name: Renewing the Canada Strong Pass, making national museums permanently free for children and youth, and supporting national museums and heritage institutions

text.topic: Arts, culture and the Productivity Mega Deduction
text.text: Budget 2026 also proposes to permanently make admission to Canada's national museums free year-round for children and youth under 25. To support this initiative, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $46.3 million over five years, starting in 2026-27, and $11.5 million ongoing to Canada's national museums and the National Battlefields Commission.

items.name: Supporting Canadian stories, journalism, and media

text.topic: Supporting Canadian stories, journalism, and media
text.text: Canadian culture finds its fullest expression in the rich stories, experiences, and perspectives we share. Seeing those reflected in the media we watch, listen to, or read strengthens our shared identity and gives Canadian creators more opportunities to flourish. Canadian stories help us understand our country and one another. When a young reader in Iqaluit, Halifax, Saskatoon, or Trois-Rivières picks up a book by a Canadian author, they see their country, and themselves, more clearly.

text.topic: Supporting Canadian stories, journalism, and media
text.text: Building on existing support for the audiovisual sector, local journalism, publishing, libraries, and digital access, these investments will help Canadian creators keep making the music, films, shows, books, and news that reflect who we are, and make that content easier to find wherever Canadians watch, listen, and read. To bring more Canadian stories to readers:

text.topic: Supporting Canadian stories, journalism, and media
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $32.2 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $9.5 million in future years, to make it easier for Canadians to discover and borrow books by Canadian authors by establishing a free national digital collection. Launching with at least 200 titles in 2027-28, the collection will grow to more than 2,000 titles, with capacity for up to 2 million loans annually by 2031-32. Funding will support licensing, an online lending platform, promotion, and outreach to help Canadian stories reach more readers.

text.topic: Supporting Canadian stories, journalism, and media
text.text: Budget 2026 also proposes to provide $20 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $5 million ongoing to renew the Canada Book Fund so Canadian publishers can bring more Canadian-authored books to readers at home and abroad and give authors, illustrators, translators, and other creators more opportunities to build lasting careers.

text.topic: Supporting Canadian stories, journalism, and media
text.text: And soon, Canadian artists will have a new international stage. Canada will participate in its first-ever Eurovision Song Contest through CBC/Radio-Canada in May 2027 in Burgas, Bulgaria. The contest is an opportunity to showcase Canadian artists to millions of viewers around the world, while giving Canadians a new opportunity to come together at home, watching and listening together.

items.name: Extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit

text.topic: Extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit
text.text: To support fact-based journalism and help sustain high-quality local news, the Spring Economic Update 2026 announced that Canada's new government would extend eligibility for the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit to audio and audiovisual news production. We have consulted stakeholders on the proposed extension; Budget 2026 was informed by that feedback. To help Canadians continue to access trusted local news and information through a wide range of media platforms:

text.topic: Extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to extend the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit to qualifying private audio and audiovisual news organisations, in line with support provided to news organisations that produce written news. They would be eligible for the same temporarily enhanced credit rate of 35% and annual labour expenditure limit of $85,000 per employee. These changes would be effective for labour expenses incurred on or after Budget Day.

text.topic: Extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit
text.text: For print journalism, Budget 2026 proposes to renew the temporarily enhanced 35% credit rate for two more years, until December 31, 2028—providing greater stability as the sector adapts to a changing media landscape. Newly eligible qualifying private audio and audiovisual news organisations would benefit from the same enhanced rate through 2028.

text.topic: Extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit
text.text: These measures would cost an estimated $501 million over five years, starting in 2026-27, and $85 million ongoing.

items.name: Promoting Francophone culture

text.topic: Promoting Francophone culture
text.text: Millions of Canadians speak French, and Francophone culture is a core part of our history, culture, and identity. As an officially bilingual country, and a leading member of the international Francophonie, Canada plays an important role in promoting the French language at home and abroad. Canada's diverse Francophone communities, including Quebecers, Acadians, Franco-Ontarians, Franco-Manitobans, and many others across the country, keep French language and culture vibrant in Canada. We are committed to supporting this integral part of our nation's history, present, and future. It means using our Presidency of the Francophonie to promote the French language and culture in all formats and enhancing discoverability.

text.topic: Promoting Francophone culture
text.text: In 2028, Canada will host the Francophonie Summit for the first time in two decades, bringing together up to 90 member states in the National Capital Region. With its longstanding Francophone communities and role as the seat of Canada's national, bilingual institutions, the National Capital Region is a fitting place to welcome the international Francophonie to Canada. The Summit will showcase the diversity and vitality of Canada's Francophone cultures and strengthen connections among Francophone communities across Canada and around the world. It will also prioritise the protection and promotion of the French language in the age of social media and artificial intelligence.

text.topic: Promoting Francophone culture
text.text: We will work closely with provincial, territorial, and municipal partners to deliver a successful summit, led by Global Affairs Canada and supported by federal partners including Canadian Heritage and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Hosting the Summit is expected to attract visitors and investment, generate opportunities for Canadian businesses and creators, and support stronger economic and cultural ties across the Francophonie.

text.text: To advance Canada's Francophonie leadership objectives, as well as support the logistics and security required to host the 2028 Francophonie Summit, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $393.2 million over three years, starting in 2027-28, on a cash basis, to 10 departments and agencies.

text.topic: Preserving the legacy of those who have served Canada
text.text: For nearly a century, the National Field of Honour in Pointe-Claire, Québec, has honoured the service and sacrifice of Canadian and allied veterans. More than 20,000 veterans and family members are honourably laid to rest amid the maple trees and granite plaques of this national historic site.

text.topic: Preserving the legacy of those who have served Canada
text.text: There, families, friends, and visitors can walk its grounds, learn about Canada's military history, and pay their respects. This site has long been operated by the Last Post Fund. But faced with growing financial pressures and the need for significant upgrades and environmental remediation, the Last Post Fund has asked the Government of Canada to assume ownership so that the site may continue to serve as an important link to our past.

text.topic: Preserving the legacy of those who have served Canada
text.text: We are committed to ensuring that the National Field of Honour remains a dignified and respectful resting place for veterans and that future generations have a place to learn about and honour those who served Canada.

text.topic: Preserving the legacy of those who have served Canada
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $15.9 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $2.1 million ongoing to Veterans Affairs Canada to acquire, remediate, and operate the National Field of Honour.

text.topic: Preserving the legacy of those who have served Canada
text.text: Honouring those who served means ensuring that their stories of courage, service, and sacrifice are passed on to future generations of Canadians. In the coming years, Canada will commemorate several defining moments in its military history. These include the 110th anniversaries of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, a foundational moment in Canada's national story, and the Battle of Passchendaele, as well as the 85th anniversary of the Dieppe Raid. These commemorations will bring Canadians together to pay tribute to the men and women who served Canada, deepen public understanding of their contributions, and ensure that their service and sacrifice are remembered for generations to come.

text.topic: Supporting Canada's national parks and historic sites
text.text: Canada is home to breathtaking national parks and historic sites where Canadians can walk amid our past. Canada's public institutions help protect and share some of our country's most significant places, collections, and experiences. That is why we are renewing these assets: to ensure they remain available for future generations and continue to help Canadians discover—and rediscover—our home.

Together, these investments will support Parks Canada's management of over 20,000 assets located in more than 200 national parks, national marine conservation areas, and national historic sites.

text.topic: Investing in our oceans
text.text: Canada is shaped by water. From the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River to the three oceans that surround us, our waterways connect communities, sustain livelihoods, and link Canada to the world. We are an ocean nation, with the world's longest coastline and a culture shaped by how we enjoy, use, and depend on our waters. That is why Canada has an important responsibility to protect its marine ecosystems, secure its coastal waters, and support a sustainable ocean economy.

text.text: In September 2026, we announced a historic $1.2 billion over four years, starting in 2027-28, to better protect our oceans and the life they sustain. items.name: Investing in housing and infrastructure in First Nations communities – Investments in First Nations clean water infrastructure and legislation

text.topic: Investing in housing and infrastructure in First Nations communities
text.text: Every person living in Canada should have access to clean and safe drinking water, adequate housing, and dependable infrastructure, but for too many First Nations communities, clean water remains out of reach. Closing these gaps is essential to supporting healthy communities, a good quality of life, and economic opportunities.

text.topic: Investing in housing and infrastructure in First Nations communities
text.text: Clean water is foundational to communities. That is why we are working to end all long-term drinking water advisories on First Nations reserves. To achieve this, we introduced Bill C-37, the proposed First Nations Clean Water Act and, as announced in June 2026, are investing $4.6 billion over five years, starting in 2026-27, to improve water and wastewater infrastructure. Between April 2025 and September 30, 2026, 11 long-term drinking water advisories were lifted, and 44 short-term advisories were lifted before becoming long-term.

text.topic: New investments in First Nations housing and infrastructure
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to build on these investments through a significant long-term funding commitment of $32 billion over 10 years for First Nations housing and infrastructure. A sustained, 10-year commitment focused on providing greater certainty, accelerating construction, and transforming the way projects are financed would help communities make strategic investments and progressively close housing and infrastructure gaps over time.

text.topic: To accelerate and maintain housing construction:
text.text: To improve First Nations housing, Budget 2026 proposes to provide $11 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28. This funding will help communities manage and preserve 119,000 existing housing units through regular maintenance and repairs, construct more than 6,900 new homes, and renovate more than 10,900 existing homes over the next decade.

text.topic: Supporting student success in First Nations communities
text.text: All Indigenous children in Canada should have access to high-quality education that respects and embraces their culture. Federal investments in First Nations-led kindergarten to Grade 12 education on reserve are producing strong results. Since last year, we have supported 541 First Nations-administered education programs and more than 120,820 students, helping to grow student participation, expand access to culturally grounded programming, and improve supports that enable First Nations students to reach their full potential:

text.topic: Supporting student success in First Nations communities
text.text: Enrolment is up 31% in First Nations-administered schools relative to 10 years ago, outpacing other forms of schooling.

text.topic: Supporting student success in First Nations communities
text.text: 94% of students have access to First Nations language instruction for one or more subjects, and 95% of students have access to culturally-based learning, meaning almost all children now have access to culturally-enriched programming.

text.topic: Supporting student success in First Nations communities
text.text: There are 115% more students in First Nations-administered kindergarten programs than in 2016-17, reflecting that more First Nations schools now have the resources needed to broaden the type of education they provide.

text.topic: Supporting student success in First Nations communities
text.text: Over 41,000 students across 195 First Nations school programs have been supported by the National School Food Program, which we recently made permanent. This is helping ensure that First Nations children have access to healthy meals and snacks at school, and can reach their full potential in the classroom.

text.text: Canada is committed to removing systemic barriers that make it difficult for Indigenous children and youth to access the services and supports they need.
