text.text: To support the long-term success, health, and safety of Indigenous communities, Budget 2026 proposes targeted investments to strengthen public health services, provide coverage for health products and services, support stable and culturally responsive First Nations and Inuit policing services, and advance community-led approaches to safety and well-being. text.text: We know that building Canada Strong means building together. Enhancing the financial, fiscal, and institutional capacity of Indigenous governments is essential to expanding their full participation in Canada's economy.

items.name: Advancing gender equality

text.topic: Advancing gender equality
text.text: Canada is a global leader in advancing gender equality and in innovative financing for women's rights organisations. At home, we have strengthened our support for women's organisations, including through Women and Gender Equality's Women's Program.

text.topic: Advancing gender equality
text.text: National women's rights organisations (NWROs) are essential partners in furthering equality in Canada and supporting our leadership internationally. They are an important part of Canada's policy and democratic infrastructure. They bring together women's lived experiences, generate evidence and expertise, identify systemic and emerging issues, provide front-line intelligence, contribute to policy and legal solutions, and offer an independent equality lens on government action.

text.topic: Advancing gender equality
text.text: We recognise the value of this national capacity and are committed to strengthening it. We are exploring how best to preserve the expertise, networks, and institutional knowledge that NWROs have built, so they can continue contributing to better public policy and to greater equality for women across Canada.

text.topic: Advancing gender equality
text.text: Over the years, federal actions have delivered meaningful progress toward greater gender equality. The Women's Program has supported more than 700 projects since 2018, reaching more than 400,000 women, girls, and other Canadians and helping reduce barriers to employment and education. But we are striving to build on this progress and do more to advance gender equality.

items.name: Implementing Canada's Black Justice Strategy

text.topic: Implementing Canada's Black Justice Strategy
text.text: Black Canadians continue to face systemic barriers within the criminal justice system. They are overrepresented both within the justice system and among victims of crime. Canada's Black Justice Strategy is the country's first national strategy dedicated to addressing anti-Black racism and systemic discrimination in our justice system. It provides a 10-year framework for improving justice and public safety outcomes for Black people in Canada, in direct partnership with Black communities across the country.

text.topic: Implementing Canada's Black Justice Strategy
text.text: This strategy is helping Black Canadians navigate the court system, while supporting services for victims and survivors of crime. It is also helping young people avoid or move beyond the justice system altogether, delivering culturally responsive support for people in correctional facilities and those returning to their communities, all while improving our data on disparities in the justice system.

text.topic: Implementing Canada's Black Justice Strategy
text.text: We are also working to expand economic opportunities for Black Canadians. This includes helping young people find work, strengthening Black-led, Black-focused, and Black-serving organisations, and supporting Black entrepreneurs and business owners. We have previously invested $189 million over five years, starting in 2025-26, through the Black Entrepreneurship Program.

text.topic: Implementing Canada's Black Justice Strategy
text.text: Budget 2026 continues this important work, providing additional funding to support the implementation of Canada's Black Justice Strategy. The next phase will focus on improving access to justice, reducing involvement in the justice system, reducing repeat offending, and continuing to work closely with Black communities to move the Strategy forward.

text.topic: Renewing the 2SLGBTQI+ Project Stream
text.text: All Canadians should be able to be their whole selves, love who they love, and fully enjoy their rights. The Federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan was Canada's first whole-of-government plan to advance equality for 2SLGBTQI+ communities. In 2022, the Government of Canada committed $100 million over five years to support its implementation. Since then, Canada has made important progress in advancing the rights and inclusion of 2SLGBTQI+ people. But there is more work to do to build a safer, more inclusive country for all, and we are taking action.

text.topic: Renewing the 2SLGBTQI+ Project Stream

text.topic: Renewing the 2SLGBTQI+ Project Stream
text.text: This ongoing support will provide greater stability for 2SLGBTQI+ organisations, allowing them to focus more of their efforts on serving communities, strengthening local networks, and delivering projects that improve outcomes for 2SLGBTQI+ people across Canada. We remain committed to continuing the work and advancing the priorities of the 2SLGBTQI+ National Action Plan.

items.name: Advancing the Defence Drone Initiative

text.topic: Advancing the Defence Drone Initiative
text.text: Since we launched the Defence Drone Initiative in July, it is already transforming the way defence capabilities are delivered. In just under two months, the Initiative has begun laying the foundation for a stronger sovereign national defence drone ecosystem by establishing a marketplace—an innovative new tool to create a faster pathway for promising Canadian technologies to move from concept to operational testing and, where they meet defence requirements, into production. As the nature of war rapidly evolves, driven by the proliferation of drones, autonomous systems, and weapons in orbit, Canada's drone capability is more crucial than ever before.

text.topic: Advancing the Defence Drone Initiative
text.text: Budget 2026 proposes to provide $2.3 billion over five years, starting in 2027-28, on a cash basis to the Department of National Defence for the Defence Drone Initiative to accelerate the discovery, acquisition, and deployment of uncrewed and counter-uncrewed capabilities. A portion of funding for this initiative would be sourced from funding already provisioned in the fiscal framework.

text.topic: Expanding Operation REASSURANCE
text.text: In addition to investing in new capabilities, Canada is increasing its support for Operation REASSURANCE, Canada's largest overseas deployment mission to deter Russian aggression on NATO's Eastern Flank and fortify our shared European defence. We have extended Operation REASSURANCE until 2031 and plan to increase Canada's persistently deployed personnel to up to 2,600. As part of the extension, Canada will join Latvia and Denmark as the third Framework Nation of Multinational Division North, boldly taking on more responsibility to protect NATO's Eastern Flank in Europe. Budget 2026 proposes to provide:

text.topic: Expanding Operation REASSURANCE

text.topic: Supporting Canadian Armed Forces members and their families after the Wainwright tragedy
text.text: Members of the CAF dedicate their lives to serving Canada, defending our country, and standing ready when Canadians need them most. That service demands commitment and sacrifice not only from those who wear the uniform, but also from the families who support them.

text.topic: Supporting Canadian Armed Forces members and their families after the Wainwright tragedy
text.text: The recent tragic incident at the Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in which members of the CAF were killed and others seriously wounded during a training exercise, is a harsh reminder of the risks CAF members assume in the course of their service, including while training to maintain operational readiness. These members of our armed forces served Canada. Now Canada must serve them.

text.topic: Supporting Canadian Armed Forces members and their families after the Wainwright tragedy

text.text: Launched in February 2026, the government's Security, Sovereignty and Prosperity: Canada's Defence Industrial Strategy sets out an ambitious agenda to protect Canada's sovereignty and strengthen our strategic autonomy while building greater economic prosperity here at home. The Strategy increases defence investments, while at the same time streamlining our supply chains. Through the government's Buy Canadian Policy, we are ensuring that Canadian firms are the key partners in meeting Canada's new defence and security needs. This gives Canadian defence companies the demand to scale up and invest with confidence. This also means that the Defence Industrial Strategy is another tool we are using to strengthen our economy while creating high-value jobs, building new infrastructure, and expanding Canadian defence offerings for global markets.

text.topic: Protecting Canada through sovereign intelligence
text.text: Canadians should be able to trust that their country can identify and confront threats to their security, sovereignty, and way of life. In a more volatile and dangerous world, the threat environment is becoming more complex, from foreign interference and espionage to terrorism and other challenges that cross borders. Protecting Canada and advancing our interests requires sovereign, strong intelligence capabilities.

text.topic: Protecting Canada through sovereign intelligence
text.text: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) is central to that effort. It works to identify and counter threats to Canada's national security, while providing the information and analysis needed to support sound decisions and act in Canada's interests. To strengthen Canada's ability to protect its national security and act independently in a changing threat environment:

text.topic: Making online spaces safe for everyone
text.text: The pace of technological change is rapid, and the risks Canadians face online are evolving with it. Yet, the policies and approaches that once kept Canadians safe online are no longer enough. The data is clear: online harms and exploitation are intensifying. Children and youth are particularly vulnerable, facing harms such as child sexual exploitation, cyberbullying, and self-harm that can have long-term impacts on their mental health and well-being. In 2024, Canadian police services reported 16,905 incidents of online sexual offence against children, three times higher than in 2018 and four times higher than in 2014. Canadian parents are rightly concerned about their children's safety online, while they themselves are at risk of increasingly sophisticated online crimes, which often target their finances or identities.

text.topic: Making online spaces safe for everyone
text.text: Canadians should not have to face these challenges alone. That is why we are taking action to protect Canadians from digital and financial threats and help build safer communities. In June 2026, we introduced Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, to strengthen online safety by introducing new requirements for social media services and AI chatbot services and enhancing protections for children and young people. While laws exist to respond to harms once they have occurred, Bill C-34 shifts the focus toward preventing harms in the first place and holding platforms accountable for the safety of their users.

items.name: Delivering the benefits of AI for all Canadians – AI for All

text.topic: Delivering the benefits of AI for all Canadians
text.text: AI is transforming daily life, changing how businesses operate while reshaping global economic competitiveness, productivity, and innovation. To ensure the benefits of AI are shared by all, it must be developed and used in ways that are safe, strengthen Canada's sovereignty, and protect our democracy. As one of just four countries at the forefront of the AI revolution, Canada has a generational opportunity: one that we cannot afford to miss.

text.topic: Delivering the benefits of AI for all Canadians
text.text: In June 2026, we launched Canada's National AI Strategy: AI for All. Supported by an initial investment of $2.7 billion on a cash basis, the strategy strengthens digital privacy protections, protects Canadians from the safety risks of AI, expands access to computing power for Canadian researchers and businesses, and helps homegrown AI companies access the capital they need to grow. We are committed to a future where AI is adopted responsibly, in a way that truly serves all Canadians—building trust, expanding opportunities, and reinforcing our sovereignty.

sections.name: Protecting Canadians from digital and financial threats

items.name: Delivering Canada's National Anti-Fraud Strategy

text.topic: Delivering Canada's National Anti-Fraud Strategy
text.text: Canadians are increasingly targeted by sophisticated, technology-enabled fraud. It may look like a text from a relative asking for money, or a bank's "new website" asking for credit card information. Almost instantly, Canadians can be defrauded without knowing what they did wrong until it's far too late. Fraudsters are increasingly exploiting digital platforms, telecommunications services, and the financial system. These scams undermine Canadians' confidence in our economy and profoundly threaten their financial security. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre reported losses totalling more than $704 million in 2025 alone—an amount estimated to represent only 5% to 10% of actual losses.

text.topic: Delivering Canada's National Anti-Fraud Strategy
text.text: The private sector is already taking action to address this challenge. For example, Canada's largest financial institutions and telecom companies jointly launched a Cross-Sector Anti-Fraud Exchange platform in October 2026, which will allow them to work together to identify and prevent repeat fraud as new techniques are developed.

text.topic: Delivering Canada's National Anti-Fraud Strategy
text.text: To tackle this rising threat to the financial well-being of Canadians, strong government leadership is also needed. We are developing Canada's first National Anti-Fraud Strategy, which brings together financial institutions, digital platforms, and telecommunication companies in a cross-sectoral approach to protect Canadians from fraud schemes as they evolve. Concurrently with Budget 2026, the Department of Finance Canada is publishing a policy statement outlining next steps for the Strategy.

text.text: To combat fraud and protect Canadians' bank accounts, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to:

text.topic: Delivering Canada's National Anti-Fraud Strategy
text.text: Introduce a legislated Multi-Sector Anti-Fraud Framework, as a cornerstone of the National Anti-Fraud Strategy, to enhance fraud-related protections for Canadians across the financial and telecommunications sectors and on digital platforms. To protect Canadians, organisations will be required to prevent, detect, disrupt, and respond to fraud, and to work with each other, across sectors, to resolve fraud-related complaints.

text.topic: Preparing for and responding to wildfires
text.text: Recent wildfire seasons have been among the most severe in Canadian history. This year, Canada had more than 5,400 wildfires that collectively burned approximately 4.5 million hectares of land; in total, they forced more than 33,750 people from their homes, including more than 8,800 people from Indigenous communities. Wildfires are devastating: they force people from their homes, destroy possessions, and put lives, businesses, and critical infrastructure at grave risk. Meeting the challenge posed by increasingly severe and less predictable wildfires requires greater preparedness and collaboration across all levels of government.

text.text: First Nations communities are often among the hardest hit by emergencies like wildfires. Extended evacuations can separate people from their homes, communities, and support networks for long periods of time, disrupting daily life and making recovery more difficult.

text.topic: Strengthening emergency preparedness in First Nations communities
text.text: That is why Budget 2026 contains measures to help communities respond, recover, and prepare by strengthening emergency management support, expanding wildfire protection, and investing in First Nations-led fire safety priorities. In October 2026, we announced:

text.text: To strengthen Canada's ability to respond to these rare events and allow insurers to focus on helping Canadian households and businesses recover when support is most needed, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to:

items.name: Making it easier for Canadians to manage their taxes

text.topic: Making it easier for Canadians to manage their taxes
text.text: Every year, Canadians spend hours navigating complex tax rules, deadlines, and payment requirements. To save Canadians time and effort while making it easier for them to meet their tax obligations, Budget 2026 proposes to:

text.topic: Making it easier for Canadians to manage their taxes
text.text: Amend the Income Tax Act to increase the instalment thresholds, which have not changed since 2008, to $7,500 and index them to inflation. In addition, Budget 2026 proposes to simplify the instalment regime for self-employed business owners, including by allowing them to make a single payment of two thirds of their net tax owing by December 31. As a result, nearly 1.1 million individuals and 185,000 small incorporated businesses would no longer pay taxes in instalments. This would also reduce the compliance burden for 190,000 self-employed individuals. This measure would apply to 2028 and subsequent taxation years.

text.topic: Making it easier for Canadians to manage their taxes
text.text: This measure ensures that Canadians can focus on the things that matter—not filling out unnecessary forms and paperwork.

text.topic: Connecting more Canadians to federal benefits
text.text: We are working to make it easier for Canadians to file their taxes and receive the benefits to which they are entitled, including the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, the Canada Child Benefit, and the Canada Workers Benefit.

text.topic: Connecting more Canadians to federal benefits
text.text: Budget 2025 launched Automatic Federal Benefits, including pre-filled tax returns for up to 5.5 million low-income Canadians by the 2028 tax year. It also announced legislative amendments enabling the CRA to file returns on behalf of eligible lower-income Canadians with simple tax situations who do not owe tax and do not file on their own. The CRA plans to offer a pre-filled return to about one million known filers, starting in the 2027 filing season.

text.topic: Connecting more Canadians to federal benefits
text.text: To build on this progress, Budget 2026 proposes to provide the CRA with $22.3 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $5.9 million in 2031-32, to strengthen outreach with people disconnected from the tax and benefits system.

text.topic: Connecting more Canadians to federal benefits

text.text: Canadian businesses should be focused on growing, creating more jobs, and expanding their opportunities at home and abroad: they shouldn't need to waste time and resources navigating tax paperwork. We are working to simplify our tax administration and reduce compliance burdens for businesses. That way, our firms can get back to doing what they do best and create value and jobs for Canadians.

text.text: To reduce the time and effort Canadians are required to spend managing their tax affairs, Budget 2026 proposes practical changes to simplify deadlines, filings, and interactions with the CRA, ultimately reducing the time tax on Canadians:

text.topic: More flexible tax instalments
text.text: Extend the timeframe to file a notice of objection and remove the need for taxpayers to request an extension of time. Taxpayers currently have 90 days to file a notice of objection to an income tax assessment (or the later of 90 days and one year from the tax return filing due date in the case of an individual or graduated rate estate) and, in most situations, have an additional year to request an extension of time to file. Budget 2026 proposes to provide most taxpayers with one year after a notice of assessment is sent to file an objection, while individuals and graduated rate estates would have until the later of that date and two years after their tax return filing due date. This change would simplify the process for individuals and businesses and eliminate the need for the CRA to review and approve extension requests.

text.text: Canadians expect government services to be accessible, reliable, and responsive. text.topic: Strengthening the effectiveness of fines and penalties
text.text: Fines and penalties enforce the rules and regulations, but when they are treated as merely the cost of doing business, changes are needed to deter non-compliance. Following Budget 2025, we undertook a review of fines and penalties to identify where stronger deterrents are needed. Areas reviewed to date include the financial sector and the tax system, with particular attention to fines and penalties that might be outdated, inadequate, and ineffective. items.name: Renewing the public service – aligning operating budgets with ERI personnel savings

text.topic: Renewing the public service
text.text: The public service is vital to delivering results for Canadians, but for too long it grew at an unsustainable pace, outstripping the growth in the Canadian population. We took decisive action to return the public service to a sustainable level to refocus on delivering tangible outcomes and results for Canadians.

text.topic: Renewing the public service
text.text: As part of the Comprehensive Expenditure Review introduced in Budget 2025, we launched the Early Retirement Incentive (ERI) program to support the transition to a leaner, more efficient federal public service while minimising the hardship for departing federal employees. More than 10,000 applications were submitted to the ERI program between March and July 2026.

text.topic: Renewing the public service
text.text: As a further step to support a more sustainable size for the federal public service, Budget 2026 announces the government's intention to align organisational operating budgets with personnel savings generated through the ERI program. Where ERI departures exceed planned workforce reductions under the Comprehensive Expenditure Review, a portion of the resulting personnel savings would be reflected in operating budget reductions. This would help ensure savings generated through the program are sustained over time.

text.topic: Renewing the public service
text.text: Operating budget reductions resulting from this measure are expected to total $400 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, and $100 million ongoing, and reductions will be reflected in the 2027-28 Main Estimates. The ERI is part of the government's continued efforts to ensure that public sector compensation costs are fair and reasonable, while aligning with Canadian labour market trends and our fiscal position. Together, these efforts free up resources for investment in Canada: growing the economy, building major projects, and creating new high-paying careers.

text.topic: Renewing the public service
text.text: Alongside these efforts, we are also ensuring that savings from changes to employer compensation costs are reflected in the fiscal framework. Accordingly, Budget 2026 captures savings resulting from the reduction in the base Canada Pension Plan contribution rate announced in the Spring Economic Update 2026. As an employer of more than 400,000 people across the federal public service, the Canadian Armed Forces, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the federal government is expected to realise savings of $305 million over five years, beginning in 2026-27, and $78 million of ongoing savings, all without reducing the benefits that individuals currently receive.

text.topic: Modernising Canada Post
text.text: The Canada Post Corporation is a longstanding national institution that provides postal services to all Canadians. Yet the use of traditional letter mail for communication and commerce continues to decline, and Canada Post's existing model no longer works for 21st-century Canada's needs. This is why we are taking steps to improve the corporation's efficiency, accountability, and long-term financial sustainability, ensuring it continues to provide its critical services and keep our postal service delivering for Canadians. Budget 2026 proposes to:

text.topic: Modernising Canada Post
text.text: Provide additional support to Canada Post's operations including $1.4 billion over two years.

text.topic: Modernising Canada Post
text.text: Provide $1.2 billion over seven years to support the conversion of urban door-to-door mail delivery to community mailboxes. First announced in September 2025, the transition will streamline operations while maintaining high service standards and is expected to generate approximately $2.2 billion in savings over 10 years, helping put Canada Post back on the path toward financial sustainability.

text.topic: Modernising Canada Post
text.text: Help bring Canada Post's stamp pricing more closely in line with OECD peers by raising stamp rates, beginning in 2027, to $2.00 for single stamps and 7% per year continuously. This measure will have a relatively limited impact on consumers and small businesses, with an estimate of only approximately $6 per year for consumers and $9 per year for small businesses. This increase will further offset costs while ensuring continuous affordability.

text.topic: Modernising Canada Post
text.text: Increase Canada Post Corporation's Annual Reference Levels by $101.4 million from 2026-27 to 2030-31, and $28 million in future years to fund the special postage rate for library materials and for expanded postal inspections, particularly in Indigenous, northern, and remote communities.

text.text: Canada's financing Crown corporations are a key tool to help promising companies and projects succeed in Canada and expand into international markets. They are particularly important where private capital alone is unavailable to meet the needs of Canadian businesses. At the same time, the increasing number of financing Crown corporations can create confusion among clients about which best fits their needs, create overlap in service delivery, and limit opportunities to improve efficiency and better use taxpayer dollars to build a stronger economy.

text.topic: Streamlining the delivery of federal financing
text.text: To streamline the delivery of federal financing and provide greater clarity and efficiency for project proponents and companies, we completed a comprehensive mandate review of federal financing Crown corporations, as was announced in the Spring Economic Update 2026. This review assessed the mandates and approaches of various federal financing entities, including in relation to the Canada Strong Fund.

text.topic: Streamlining the delivery of federal financing

The new institution will build on the strengths, expertise, and strong teams of both organisations to provide Canadian businesses with a more integrated suite of financing solutions from domestic growth through to international expansion. A specially constituted Board of Directors will be mandated to oversee the transition, supported by further analysis and consultations with key clients and stakeholders. Existing products and services will be fully maintained throughout the transition.

mentions.topic: Instalment Payments for Individuals and Corporations
mentions.text: Most individuals pay taxes through withholdings on their employment income that are remitted to the Canada Revenue Agency by their employers. However, where an individual receives income from sources that are not subject to withholding (e.g., certain sources of pension income, business income, dividends, interest, rental income, and capital gains), they may have to pay income tax in quarterly instalments. For most individuals, instalments are required if their combined federal-provincial net tax owing on income from such sources for the current year and either of the two previous years is more than $3,000 (or $1,800 federal net tax owing for Quebec residents). The income tax instalment thresholds are lower for Quebec residents because the federal government does not collect provincial income tax in Quebec.

mentions.topic: Increasing the Instalment Thresholds
mentions.text: Budget 2026 proposes to increase the threshold from $3,000 to $7,500 for corporations and individuals resident outside Quebec, and from $1,800 to $4,500 for individuals resident in Quebec. The thresholds would be indexed to inflation and rounded to the nearest $500. Any remaining tax payable for a taxation year would be due on the applicable balance-due date.

mentions.topic: Cannabis Excise Duty Stamp

Provinces and territories would have until January 31, 2027 to confirm their participation to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue.
